howItWorks.intro: The dollar cost of any Ethereum action reduces to one relationship: gas units used, multiplied by the price you pay per unit of gas, multiplied by what ETH is worth in dollars at that moment.

rules.name: Gas Cost
rules.formula: Cost (USD) = Gas Units x Gas Price (Gwei) / 1e9 x ETH Price
rules.explanation: Convert gas units to ETH using the gas price, then multiply by the current ETH/USD exchange rate.

howItWorks.outro: Gas prices swing block to block with network demand, and ETH's dollar price moves independently and often sharply — so treat every figure above as a snapshot based on the gas price and ETH price you entered, not a live quote, and not financial or investment advice.

faq.question: Why is deployment cost so much higher than a single interaction?
faq.answer: Deployment writes your entire contract bytecode to the blockchain permanently, which costs roughly 200 gas per byte on top of the ~32,000-gas contract-creation overhead — a contract with 10,000 bytes of bytecode alone accounts for roughly 2,000,000 gas before the constructor even runs. A later function call only executes the specific opcodes that function needs, so it's typically a small fraction of the deployment cost.

faq.question: What's a realistic gas price to use for "Gas Price (Gwei)"?
faq.answer: Check a live gas tracker or your wallet's fee estimator right before you plan to transact. Ethereum mainnet gas price commonly ranges from single digits during quiet periods to 50-100+ gwei during high demand (NFT mints, major DeFi activity), and it can spike well above that during extreme congestion. Enter the combined base-fee-plus-tip figure your wallet shows, not the base fee alone.

faq.question: Why does a token swap cost more gas than sending ETH?
faq.answer: A plain ETH transfer is 21,000 gas because it does nothing but move a balance between two accounts. A swap on a decentralized exchange has to read pool reserves, run the pricing math, update two token balances, check allowances, and emit log events — each of those is separate EVM execution, which is why swaps typically run 100,000-150,000 gas, five to seven times a simple transfer.

faq.question: How do I lower my contract's gas costs?
faq.answer: For deployment, trim bytecode size — remove unused functions, avoid storing large constant strings on-chain, and share code across deployments with libraries or a proxy pattern. For interactions, minimize SSTORE operations (a cold storage write can cost 20,000+ gas by itself), pack several small values into a single 32-byte storage slot, and prefer emitting events over storing data you don't need to read back on-chain later.

faq.question: Does this calculator use live gas prices or ETH prices?
faq.answer: No — you enter both manually, and the result is only as current as the numbers you type in. Gas prices can move meaningfully within a single block, and ETH's dollar price can swing several percent in a day, so treat the output as a planning estimate for that specific input, not a live quote, and not financial advice.

faq.question: Why do deployment gas and interaction gas need separate budgets?
faq.answer: Deployment is a one-time cost paid once when the contract goes live; interaction cost recurs every time someone calls a function, and it's usually paid by whoever sends that transaction — often your users, not you. The "Avg Functions Called/Day" field projects that recurring cost separately so you can see the true monthly operating cost of a live contract, not just the upfront deployment bill.

howWeCalculate.intro: This calculator applies the same gas-to-dollar conversion validators and wallets use under the hood, run entirely in your browser against the numbers you supply.
steps: Enter your contract's deployed bytecode size in bytes — larger contracts cost more to write to the chain because of Ethereum's per-byte code-deposit fee
Enter how many times per day you expect users to call the contract's functions once it's live, so ongoing interaction cost can be projected alongside the one-time deployment cost
Enter the gas price in gwei (base fee plus priority tip) and the current ETH/USD price — both change constantly, so use the values your wallet or a gas tracker shows at the time you plan to transact
Click Calculate to convert deployment and interaction gas into ETH and USD costs instantly, with no data leaving your browser
howWeCalculate.disclaimer: These are engineering estimates for planning a deployment and its ongoing operating cost, not a substitute for simulating the exact transaction against current mainnet or testnet conditions, and not financial advice — gas and ETH prices can move significantly between when you calculate and when you actually transact.

whenToUse.intro: Reach for this calculator whenever a gas or ETH price move could change whether a deployment or a feature is still worth shipping at its current cost.
scenarios: Budgeting a contract launch, when you need to know deployment cost before committing bytecode to mainnet
Sizing the ongoing cost of a feature that calls a contract function frequently, like a DeFi protocol's swap or claim function
Comparing gas costs across different network conditions — deploying during low-congestion hours versus peak demand
Deciding whether to deploy to an L2 or sidechain instead of Ethereum mainnet, once you see what mainnet gas at current prices would cost
Explaining to a non-technical stakeholder why a contract redesign that touches more storage slots or does more computation carries real dollar cost

sections.title: What Gas Actually Measures on Ethereum
sections.body: Gas is Ethereum's unit of account for computation. Every opcode the EVM executes — an addition, a storage write, a call to another contract — has a fixed gas cost defined in the protocol, and a transaction's total gas usage is the sum of every opcode it triggers plus the base cost of including it in a block. Deploying a contract burns gas for the 21,000-gas base transaction fee, roughly 32,000 gas for contract creation itself, and about 200 gas for every byte of bytecode written to the chain, on top of whatever the constructor executes. This calculator takes four inputs — contract size in bytes, the average number of function calls you expect per day once the contract is live, the gas price in gwei, and the current ETH/USD price — and turns them into deployment gas, deployment cost, and both daily and monthly interaction costs, so you can budget a launch and its ongoing operating cost in the same pass.

sections.title: Why Gas Price and Network Congestion Move Together
sections.body: Since the London upgrade (EIP-1559), every block has a base fee denominated in gwei — one gwei equals 0.000000001 ETH — that is set algorithmically from how full the previous block was and burned outright, plus an optional priority fee, a tip, you add to get a validator to include your transaction faster. When demand for block space rises, the base fee climbs block over block until enough transactions get priced out that usage falls back toward the network's target; when the network is quiet, it decays instead. The "Gas Price (Gwei)" field in this calculator represents that combined base-fee-plus-tip rate you're willing to pay per unit of gas, which is why the same contract can cost dramatically different amounts to deploy or use depending purely on when you submit the transaction, not on anything about the contract itself.

sections.title: From Gas Units to Dollars: Reading Your Results
sections.body: Cost in ETH is gas units × gas price in gwei, divided by 1e9 to convert gwei to ETH, then × the ETH/USD price to get dollars. A simple ETH transfer always costs exactly 21,000 gas — there's no logic to execute, just a value transfer. A token swap through an automated market maker like Uniswap, by contrast, typically runs 100,000-150,000 gas because it has to read reserves, update balances in at least two token contracts, and emit events. Concretely: a swap using 150,000 gas at a combined base-fee-plus-tip price of 30 gwei costs 150,000 × 30 gwei = 4,500,000 gwei = 0.0045 ETH; at an ETH price of $3,200 that's about $14.40 for the transaction — versus a plain 21,000-gas ETH transfer at the same 30 gwei price, which costs only 0.00063 ETH, about $2.02. Deployment cost scales mostly with bytecode size and constructor complexity, while ongoing interaction cost scales with how often each function is called, which is exactly what the "Avg Functions Called/Day" field lets you project. Keep in mind that both gas prices and ETH's dollar price are highly volatile and change block to block — this tool estimates cost from the specific gas price and ETH price you type in at one point in time, not a live quote, and nothing here is financial advice.

howToSteps.title: Enter Your Contract Size (bytes)
howToSteps.description: Start with your contract's deployed bytecode size — this is the main driver of one-time deployment gas because Ethereum charges roughly 200 gas for every byte written to the chain.

howToSteps.title: Fill In Gas Price, ETH Price, and Daily Calls
howToSteps.description: Add the current gas price in gwei, the ETH/USD price, and how many times per day you expect functions to be called — these determine both your deployment cost and your ongoing interaction costs.

howToSteps.title: Click Calculate
howToSteps.description: Run the numbers. The calculator converts gas units to ETH using your gas price, then to dollars using your ETH price, entirely in your browser.

howToSteps.title: Review Your Results
howToSteps.description: Check deployment gas, deployment cost, and daily/monthly interaction cost together — a contract can be cheap to deploy but expensive to run, or vice versa, depending on how storage-heavy each function call is.

tips: Contract size drives deployment cost almost linearly — trimming bytecode (fewer inlined libraries, smaller strings, tighter storage layout) directly lowers the code-deposit gas you pay.
Gas price shifts by the hour. Check a live gas tracker before you deploy, then plug that gwei figure in here rather than assuming yesterday's price still holds.
Interaction cost adds up fast at scale — a function that costs a few cents per call becomes real money once thousands of users call it daily, so model "Avg Functions Called/Day" realistically.
ETH's dollar price moves independently of gas price, so a cheap-gas moment can still be an expensive-dollar moment if ETH has rallied — check both inputs together, not separately.
If storage writes are the biggest cost driver in your contract, look at packing struct fields into fewer 32-byte slots — SSTORE is one of the most expensive opcodes in the EVM.
